en: Petavatthu,
Ubbarivagga, 8.
Cūḷaseṭṭhipetavatthu (The Story of the Lesser Treasurer’s Ghost)
“Bhante, you have gone forth naked and emaciated;
where do you go at night, and for what reason?
Tell us that, so that we might also be able [to practice].”
“With all my wealth, I shall provide for you.
“The city of Bārāṇasī resounds from afar;
there, householder, I was once wealthy but have now become destitute.”
One who does not give, whose mind is greedy for material things,
and who has fallen into the realm of Yama due to immorality,
is tormented by those very [actions] as if by a needle.
For that very reason, I go among my kinsmen for the sake of some small material gift;
yet they are of a nature not to give and lack faith,
[thinking] that the fruit of giving occurs only in the world beyond.
And my daughter constantly says,
"I will give an offering to my fathers and grandfathers";
when it has been prepared, the brahmins serve it out.
“I am going to Andhakavinda to eat.
To him the king said: “After you have enjoyed that as well, you may come quickly; I too shall perform an offering for you.”
"Explain that to me if there is a cause;
let us hear words of a cause that can be trusted.
Having said "So be it," he went there.
They ate their meal, yet they were not worthy of offerings;
returning once more to Rājagaha,
he appeared before the lord of men.
Seeing that he had returned once more, the king said: "What shall I give you as well?
Tell me that, if there is a reason."
“By which you might be nourished for a longer time.
“O King, having served the Buddha and the Saṅgha with food, drink, and robes,”
"Point out that offering to me for my benefit,
so that I may be satisfied for a longer time. Then the king, having immediately prostrated himself, said:
Having personally given incomparable gifts to the Saṅgha,
he announced what he had prepared to the Tathāgata and dedicated the merit to that deceased person.
Thus honored and appearing exceedingly resplendent,
he manifested before the lord of men:
"I am a yakkha who has attained supreme psychic power."
There are no human beings equal to me.
Behold this immeasurable majesty of mine,
which arose from giving that incomparable gift to the Saṅgha under your guidance.
"Constantly and always satisfied by many [offerings],
I go about happy among humans and devas.
The Story of the Cūḷaseṭṭhi Petas, the eighth.
The first recitation section.
